title: Introduction to Managerial Economics, Principles and Optimization Techniques

slides.visual_text: Course Contents (with a DO NOT COPY watermark). Unit-I: Introduction to Business Economics: Nature and scope; Objectives and Theory of the firm, Economic way of thinking, Optimization techniques & economic decision making. Unit-II: Demand Analysis: Utility; Demand & Supply, Law and functions; Market equilibrium; Consumer surplus, Producer surplus; Price controls and government interventions; Elasticity of demand, Determinants, Methods and managerial applications; Theory of consumer behavior, Indifference curve analysis, Budget constraint, Consumer's equilibrium; Price, Income and Substitution Effects. Unit-III: Demand forecasting: Purpose, Quantitative and qualitative techniques; Criteria for good forecasting method. Unit-IV: Production Analysis: Cost concepts; Production function, Linear, Leontief and Cobb-Douglas; Law of variable proportions and Law of returns to scale; Iso-quant and Iso-cost curve, Producer's equilibrium; Least-cost combination, Optimum input substitution, multi-product cost functions; Industry Analysis, structure-conduct-performance paradigm; Cost-oriented pricing methods. Unit-V: Market Analysis: Perfect competition, Monopoly, Monopolistic competition and Oligopoly; Output and pricing decisions; Profit, Entry and exit decisions, Short-run and long-run dynamics, Game Theory, Strategic behavior, Global Economic Climate, competition and economic growth.

Text Books: 1. Mankiw, N. G. (2014). Principles of Microeconomics. United States: Cengage Learning. 2. Petersen, H. C., Lewis, W. C., and Jain, S. K. (2006). Managerial Economics. India: Pearson Education. 3. Baye, M. R., Prince, J. (2021). Managerial Economics and Business Strategy. United Kingdom: McGraw-Hill Education. 4. Salvatore, D. (2012). Managerial Economics: Principles and Worldwide Applications. United Kingdom: Oxford University Press.

Evaluation Criteria table (Components, Weightage, Remarks): Mid semester exam (MST) and End semester exam (EST), 70%, MST 30% and EST 40%; Individual project, 10%, Individual Presentation 10%; Group project, 10%, Group Project Report 10%; In-class assignment, 10%, Case Analysis 10%.

slides.title: What is Economics?
slides.text:
What is Economics?
Economics is the study of the nature and causes of the wealth of nations
Adam Smith (1776)
Economics is a study of man in the ordinary business of life; it examines that part of individual and social action which is most closely connected with the attainment and use of the material requisites of well-being.
Alfred Marshall (1890)
Economics is the science which studies human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses.
Lionel Robbins (1932)
Economics is the study of how societies use scarce resources to produce valuable commodities and distribute them among different people, examined across time and often employing insights from history.
Paul Samuelson (1948)

slides.title: Different types of costs
slides.text:
Different types of costs
Accounting Costs
The explicit costs of the resources needed to produce produce goods or services.
Reported on the firm’s income statement.
Examples: wages, rent, electricity, raw materials
Opportunity Cost
The cost of the explicit and implicit resources that are foregone when a decision is made.
Examples: owner's time, foregone salary, own building used for business
Economic Profits
Total revenue minus total opportunity cost.
Provides a complete measure of profitability

slides.title: Understanding Incentives
slides.text:
Understanding Incentives
Managers use incentives to encourage employees to work toward organizational goals.
Example: Sales Representative
Firm's goal: Increase sales.
Employee's incentive: Earn a sales commission.
Result: Higher effort → Higher sales → Higher earnings for the employee and higher profits for the firm.
Effective managers design incentives that align employees' interests with organizational goals.

slides.title: Understand time value of money
slides.text:
Understand time value of money
Business decisions are long horizon, the value of money today will differ from tomorrow.
Would you prefer ₹10,000 today or ₹10,000 one year from now? Why?
The opportunity cost of receiving ₹10,000 one year from now is the amount of interest foregone that could be earned from investing ₹10,000 today.

slides.title: Time value of money
slides.text: Time value of money
slides.visual_text: Heading: Time value of money. Future Value (FV): Value of money at a future date after earning interest. Present Value (PV): Current value of money to be received in the future. Formula: PV = FV / (1 + i)^n, where PV = Present Value, FV = Future Value, i = Interest rate, n = Number of periods.

slides.title: Time value of money
slides.text:
Time value of money
The present value (PV) reflects the difference between the future value and the
opportunity cost of waiting (OCW).
Succinctly, PV = FV – OCW
If i = 0, note PV = FV.
As ‘i’ increases, the higher is the OCW and the lower the PV.

slides.title: Question
slides.text:
Question
Suppose you receive ₹1,100 after a year. If the interest rate is 10%, what is its value today (present value)?

bullets.text: Suppose you receive ₹1,100 after a year. If the interest rate is 10%, what is its value today (present value)?

slides.visual_text: Text only: Question. Suppose you receive ₹1,100 after a year. If the interest rate is 10%, what is its value today (present value)?

slides.title: Solution
slides.text: Solution
slides.visual_text: Heading: Solution. Future Value (FV): ₹1,100. Time (n): 1 year. Interest rate (i): 10%. Present value (PV) = FV / (1+i)^n = 1,100 / (1 + 0.10) = ₹1,000.

slides.title: Present Value of a Series
slides.text: Present Value of a Series
slides.visual_text: Heading: Present Value of a Series. Present value of a stream of future amounts (FV_t) received at the end of each period for n periods: PV = FV_1/(1 + i)^1 + FV_2/(1 + i)^2 + ... + FV_n/(1 + i)^n. Equivalently, PV = sum from t=1 to n of FV/(1+i) (the slide's summation is printed with subscript and power 1 rather than t).

slides.title: Practice Question
slides.text:
Practice Question
As marketing manager for a major automaker, you are evaluating three advertising intensities for a new SUV. Expected year-end profits (in $ millions) are given in table below. The firm's opportunity cost of funds is 10 percent. Which advertising intensity maximizes the value of the firm?

bullets.text: As marketing manager for a major automaker, you are evaluating three advertising intensities for a new SUV. Expected year-end profits (in $ millions) are given in table below. The firm's opportunity cost of funds is 10 percent. Which advertising intensity maximizes the value of the firm?

slides.visual_text: Heading: Practice Question. As marketing manager for a major automaker, you are evaluating three advertising intensities for a new SUV. Expected year-end profits (in $ millions) are given in table below. The firm's opportunity cost of funds is 10 percent. Which advertising intensity maximizes the value of the firm? Table (Advertising Intensity, Year 1, Year 2, Year 3): High 20, 95, 275; Moderate 35, 80, 155; Low 75, 110, 130.

slides.title: Solution
slides.text: Solution
slides.visual_text: Heading: Solution. Discount each year's profit back at 10% and sum. High: PV = 20/(1.10)^1 + 95/(1.10)^2 + 275/(1.10)^3 = $303.3. Moderate: PV = 35/(1.10)^1 + 80/(1.10)^2 + 155/(1.10)^3 = $214.39. Low: PV = 75/(1.10)^1 + 110/(1.10)^2 + 130/(1.10)^3 = $256.76. Ranking: High ($303.31M) > Low ($256.76M) > Moderate ($214.39M). Decision: The high advertising intensity maximizes the present value of the firm, even though it has the lowest profits in Years 1-2, the much larger Year 3 payoff more than compensates once discounted. Always compare full discounted streams, not single-year snapshots.

slides.title: Net Present Value
slides.text: Net Present Value
slides.visual_text: Heading: Net Present Value. Sum of the present values of all future cash flows from a project, minus the initial cost. Suppose a manager can purchase a stream of future receipts (FV_t) by spending C_0 dollars today. The NPV of such a decision is = FV_1/(1+i)^1 + FV_2/(1+i)^2 + ... + FV_n/(1+i)^n - C_0. If: NPV < 0: Reject project (in red); NPV > 0: Accept project (in green).

slides.title: Question
slides.text:
Question
A machine costs $5,000 today and will generate $2,000 at the end of each of the next 3 years. At an interest rate of 7%, what is the NPV? Should the firm buy it?

bullets.text: A machine costs $5,000 today and will generate $2,000 at the end of each of the next 3 years. At an interest rate of 7%, what is the NPV? Should the firm buy it?

slides.title: Solution
slides.text: Solution
slides.visual_text: Heading: Solution. FV = $2000, i = 7%, Cost = $5000. PV = 2000/(1.07)^1 + 2000/(1.07)^2 + 2000/(1.07)^3 = $5,248.63. NPV = PV - Cost. NPV = 5,248.63 - 5000 = $248.63. Decision: NPV > 0, firm should buy the machine.

slides.title: Present Value of a Perpetuity
slides.text: Present Value of a Perpetuity
slides.visual_text: Heading: Present Value of a Perpetuity. An asset that perpetually generates a stream of cash flows (CF_i) at the end of each period is called a perpetuity. The present value (PV) of a perpetuity of cash flows paying the same amount (CF = CF_1 = CF_2 = ...) at the end of each period is: PV_perpetuity = CF/(1+i)^1 + CF/(1+i)^2 + CF/(1+i)^3 + ... = CF/i.

Question

slides.visual_text: Text only: Question. An investment pays $500 at the end of every year, forever. If the interest rate is 5%, what is its present value?

slides.title: Solution
slides.text: Solution
slides.visual_text: Heading: Solution. CF = 500, i = 0.05. PV_perpetuity = CF/i = 500/0.05 = $10,000.

slides.title: Firm Valuation and Profit Maximization
slides.text: Firm Valuation and Profit Maximization
slides.visual_text: Heading: Firm Valuation and Profit Maximization. The value of a firm equals the present value of current and future profits (cash flows). PV_firm = π0 + π1/(1+i)^1 + π2/(1+i)^2 + π3/(1+i)^3 + ... A common assumption among economist is that it is the firm's goal to maximization profits. Sub-point: This means the present value of current and future profits, so the firm is maximizing its value.

slides.title: Question
slides.text:
Question
A firm generates constant annual profits of $50,000, paid out entirely as dividends, forever. If the current profits have yet to be paid out as dividends and the appropriate interest rate is 10%, what is the value of the firm?

bullets.text: A firm generates constant annual profits of $50,000, paid out entirely as dividends, forever. If the current profits have yet to be paid out as dividends and the appropriate interest rate is 10%, what is the value of the firm?

slides.title: Solution
slides.text: Solution
slides.visual_text: Heading: Solution. The firm pays out its entire profit as a dividend every year, forever, and that dividend never changes. It stays at $50,000 indefinitely. The $50,000 hasn't been paid to the owner yet. It will be paid at the end of this year. Therefore, no current payments exist. π0 = 0; π = $50,000; i = 10%. PV_firm = π0 + π/i. PV_firm = 0 + 50,000/0.10 = $500,000.

slides.title: Firm Valuation With Profit Growth
slides.text: Firm Valuation With Profit Growth
slides.visual_text: Heading: Firm Valuation With Profit Growth. If profits grow at a constant rate (g) and current period profits are π0, then: PV_firm = π0 (1+i)/(i-g); before current profits have been paid out as dividends. PV_firm = π0 (1+g)/(i-g); immediately after current profits are paid out as dividends. Both formulas are shown in red.

slides.title: Question
slides.text:
Question
A firm's current profits are $20,000 and are expected to grow at 3% per year, forever. The firm's dividends equal its profits. If the interest rate is 10%, what is the value of the firm? What is its value immediately after it pays a dividend equal to current profits?

bullets.text: A firm's current profits are $20,000 and are expected to grow at 3% per year, forever. The firm's dividends equal its profits. If the interest rate is 10%, what is the value of the firm? What is its value immediately after it pays a dividend equal to current profits?

slides.title: Solution
slides.text:
Solution
•
slides.visual_text: Heading: Solution, in two boxes. Case 1: Value of the firm. π = 20,000; g = 3%; i = 10%. PV_firm = π0 (1+i)/(i-g). PV_firm = 20,000 * (1+0.10)/(0.10-0.03) = $314,285.71. Case 2: Value of the firm immediately after it pays dividend equal to profits. π = 20,000; g = 3%; i = 10%. PV_firm = π0 (1+g)/(i-g). PV_firm = 20,000 * (1+0.03)/(0.10-0.03) = $294,285.71.

slides.title: Thinking at margin
slides.text: Thinking at margin
slides.visual_text: Heading: Thinking at margin. Managers make decisions by comparing the additional (incremental) benefits and additional (incremental) costs of an action, incremental behaviour. Marginal Benefit (MB): The additional benefit gained from taking one more unit of an action. Marginal Cost (MC): The additional cost incurred from taking one more unit of an action. Take an action only if: Marginal Benefit > Marginal Cost (in a box).

slides.title: Thinking at margin
slides.text:
Thinking at margin
Examples
Should the firm produce one more unit of a product?
Should it hire one more worker?
Should it spend ₹10,000 more on advertising?
Answer: Only if the additional benefit exceeds the additional cost.

slides.title: Marginal Principle
slides.text:
Marginal Principle
To maximize net benefits, the managerial control variable should be increased up to the point where MB = MC.
MB > MC means the last unit of the control variable increased benefits more than it increased costs.
MB < MC means the last unit of the control variable increased costs more than it increased benefits.

slides.title: The Geometry of Optimization
slides.text: The Geometry of Optimization
slides.visual_text: Heading: The Geometry of Optimization. Two graphs. Left graph: vertical axis Total Benefits & Total Costs, horizontal axis Q. A straight black Benefits line from the origin (labelled Slope = MB) and a red Costs curve that starts above zero, rises slowly then steeply. At Q* a blue dashed tangent to the Costs curve (labelled Slope = MC) is parallel to the Benefits line; at Q* benefits are B and costs are C on the vertical axis, so the vertical gap between them is largest there. Right graph: vertical axis Net Benefits, horizontal axis Q. A red hill-shaped curve rising to a peak at Q* and then falling; at the peak a flat horizontal tangent labelled Slope = MNB, with an arrow pointing to the peak labelled Maximum net benefits.

slides.title: Discrete vs. Continuous Decisions
slides.text:
Discrete vs. Continuous Decisions
Managers make two types of decisions.
We use tables for discrete decisions and calculus for continuous decisions.

bullets.text: Managers make two types of decisions.
We use tables for discrete decisions and calculus for continuous decisions.

slides.visual_text: Heading: Discrete vs. Continuous Decisions. Managers make two types of decisions. Two columns. Discrete Decisions: Choices are made in whole units; No calculus required; Marginal values computed from changes; Examples: Hire one more worker, Open another store. Continuous Decisions: Choices can take any value; Calculus is used; Marginal values computed using derivatives; Examples: Set the selling price, Decide advertising expenditure. We use tables for discrete decisions and calculus for continuous decisions.

slides.text: Computing MR, MC and profit maximising output
slides.visual_text: Heading: Computing MR, MC and profit maximising output. Table (Output (q), TR, TC, MR, MC, Marginal Profit): 0, 0, 20, -, -, -; 1, 50, 40, 50, 20, 30; 2, 100, 70, 50, 30, 20; 3, 150, 110, 50, 40, 10; 4, 200, 160, 50, 50, 0; 5, 250, 220, 50, 60, -10; 6, 300, 290, 50, 70, -20. Right side: Marginal Revenue (MR): Additional revenue from selling one more unit. MR_q = TR_q - TR_(q-1). Marginal Cost (MC): Additional cost of producing one more unit. MC_q = TC_q - TC_(q-1). Marginal Profit_q = MR_q - MC_q. Decision Rule: Produce another unit if MR > MC; Stop when MR = MC; At this point marginal profit is also maximised.

slides.title: Continuous Decisions
slides.text: Continuous Decisions
slides.visual_text: Heading: Continuous Decisions. Instead of tables, we use mathematical functions. Suppose TR = f(Q), TC = f(Q). Then, profit π(Q) = TR(Q) - TC(Q). For arriving at marginal quantities, differentiate this equation.

slides.title: Marginal Analysis Using Calculus
slides.text: Marginal Analysis Using Calculus
slides.visual_text: Heading: Marginal Analysis Using Calculus. Differentiate: dπ/dQ = dTR/dQ - dTC/dQ. Recognize that MR = dTR/dQ and MC = dTC/dQ. Decision Rule. First Order Condition: Profit is maximized when dπ/dQ = 0, Or Marginal Revenue = Marginal Cost. And, Second Order Condition: Profit function is increasing (or equivalently, the second-order condition for a maximum is satisfied). d²π/dQ² < 0.

slides.title: Profit maximization by marginal principle: Continuous choices
slides.text: Profit maximization by marginal principle: Continuous choices
slides.visual_text: Heading: Profit maximization by marginal principle: Continuous choices. Question: The Total Revenue of a firm is given as: TR = 50Q - Q². Its Total Cost is given as: TC = 10Q. Find the profit-maximizing quantity and maximum profit for the firm.

slides.title: Solution
slides.text: Solution
slides.visual_text: Heading: Solution. TR = 50Q - Q², TC = 10Q. Then, profit: π(Q) = TR(Q) - TC(Q) → 50Q - Q² - 10Q. First order condition for profit maximisation: Differentiate π(Q) and set it equal to zero; dπ/dQ = dTR/dQ - dTC/dQ = 0 → MR - MC = 0 → MR = MC. MR = 50Q - 2Q; MC = 10 [MR is printed as 50Q - 2Q on the slide]. MR = MC → 50Q - 2Q = 10 → Q = 20 (in red). Second order condition: d²π/dQ² < 0; Differentiating, we get: d²π/dQ² = -2 < 0. Profits are maximised at Q = 20 (in red). Value of profits if Q = 20: 50Q - Q² - 10Q = 50 * 20 - 20 * 20 - 10 * 20 = $400 (in red).

slides.title: Conclusion
slides.text:
Conclusion
Make sure you include all costs and benefits when making decisions (opportunity cost).
When decisions span time, make sure you are comparing apples to apples (PV analysis).
Optimal economic decisions are made at the margin (marginal analysis).
